prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which many atoms are interrogated at the magic wavelength, opening a new regime of precision in the measurement of time

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock as a single-part prize to Katori and Ye, and I have not changed my preferred configuration after reading the full exchange. The chair asks whether the lattice clock is a distinct invention after 2005 and 2012. My answer is that it is, for a reason I can state in experimental terms. A single trapped ion has small systematic shifts but one particle, so reaching a given statistical uncertainty takes very long averaging. A neutral-atom clock with a million atoms has the signal-to-noise to do this quickly, but only if the light shift from the trapping field and the Doppler and recoil shifts are all removed. The magic-wavelength condition together with Lamb-Dicke confinement in a lattice does exactly that, and it is a concept, not a refinement of the comb or of ion control. The comb counts optical cycles, and ion control gives one good reference; neither supplies this. The result has also been reproduced in many independent laboratories and intercompared over fibre at the 1e-18 level, and it has opened measurements that were not available before, such as millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, relativistic geodesy and searches for varying constants and dark-matter candidates. On attribution, Katori made the proposal and the first strontium lattice clock, and Ye took it to the accuracy and stability frontier and into many-body clock physics. Two names are compact and traceable. For the citation I would name the invention and the realization, not a record number, so that the credit stays anchored to the concept and does not drift to whoever holds the latest record.
statement.case_against: Novelty relative to the 2005 and 2012 prizes remains the strongest objection, and I cannot make it disappear by wording alone; it is a judgment of how much weight the lattice and magic-wavelength concept deserves. Attribution is the second risk. Lemonde, Takamoto, Boyd and the SYRTE, PTB and NIST groups all made real early contributions, and Ye's results rest on comb and laser-stabilization technology and a large JILA team. I regard the later groups as having confirmed and refined, but I have not verified priority dates for the early strontium and ytterbium demonstrations, and the committee should obtain an expert check before the vote. Finally the redefinition of the second has not happened. I do not think it is a precondition for a prize, but it is fair to say that waiting would make the practical consequence more visible.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B008 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) as a clean theory-then-experiment story with the broadest opening support, and with Kroll raised a possible B035 plus B008 pairing.
responses.response: I have tested the pairing you and I mentioned, and I do not think it works within a three-person ceiling: two clock names plus three topological names is five people, and trimming either side to fit would create a credit problem that is worse than the one we are trying to avoid. A two-part prize would force us to drop Mele or Molenkamp, or to drop Ye or Katori, and I do not see a principled way to do that. I therefore keep a single part. On B008 itself, I respect that the Z2 state is a new state of matter and that the quantization measurements are quantitative. My remaining difficulty is the one you name yourself: the HgTe proposal came from Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and the 3D generalization lies outside the trio. I would need the condensed-matter members to tell me that Kane and Mele plus Molenkamp is a defensible reading of who made the discovery, not just of who is most cited. If that argument is made convincingly I would support B008 as a close second, and that is why it stays as my first alternative.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B023 (IceCube) because nature gave an unexpected result, and regards B035 as chiefly a gain in precision rather than a discovery.
responses.response: I understand the criterion, and I am not dismissing it: a diffuse astrophysical neutrino flux was not predicted at that level, and the detector is also a major achievement. But I would not accept that a measurement technique that moves precision by two orders of magnitude is only a gain in precision. Several of the systematic effects that the lattice clock removed were thought to limit neutral atoms in principle, and the resulting stability allows measurements of gravitational potential differences and tests of constants that were out of reach. From my own field, measurement capability of that kind is where new discoveries have come from. My honest difficulty with B023 is the one you concede: three names against a collaboration of hundreds with AMANDA and DUMAND precursors, and point-source identifications that are still moderate in significance. I have moved B023 up to my second alternative because your argument about the diffuse flux is stronger than I allowed in round 1, but I still cannot judge from here that Halzen, Karle and Spiering is a fair trio, and I would want the expert report on credit that you and the chair mention.

responses.point: Lindroth prefers B035 and applies a standard of surprise about nature, noting that lattice clocks could be seen as a refinement of earlier ideas and that the pending redefinition of the second has not happened.
responses.response: We agree on the configuration, and I am glad you say that the magic wavelength, blackbody shift and other corrections rest on atomic-structure calculations that were repeatedly checked, since that is the part of the evidence that I would rely on in a citation defence. On the surprise standard I would answer slightly differently from you: the lattice clock came from a proposal that looked unlikely to work until it was shown that the light shift could be cancelled at a specific wavelength, and that is a result about how atoms behave in a field, not only an engineering step. I would be willing to see the citation include the magic-wavelength lattice explicitly, which is how the novelty question is answered on the page. I also take your point about Lemonde, Takamoto and Boyd; I would not add names, because the ceiling and the clarity of the pair matter, but I would ask for a check on priority before we vote.

responses.point: Pearce as chair lists the redefinition of the second as a question for round 2 and holds, with Kroll, that it is not required for a prize.
responses.response: I maintain that the redefinition is not required, because the physics and the intercomparisons are established whether or not the CIPM acts. Eriksson and Danielsson suggest it would be a more natural moment, and that is fair as a matter of timing, but it would mean tying our decision to a metrological committee schedule that we do not control. On the disclosure question: I do not think anyone needs to step back from B035 on the evidence given so far. I will repeat my own tie below so that the committee can decide this openly.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the magic-wavelength lattice with many-atom interrogation as a distinct invention rather than a continuation of the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes; this is a judgment and not a fact I can check.

Priority and fair credit among Katori, Ye, Lemonde, Takamoto, Boyd and the SYRTE and PTB groups for the early strontium and ytterbium demonstrations; I have not verified dates myself and would welcome an expert report.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second makes the prize more natural later; I do not think it is required.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. During my PhD I spent a year in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Jun Ye is a JILA colleague in Hall's circle, so I have a loose professional link to that environment; I know of no collaboration with, or supervision of, Ye or Katori. I leave it to the committee and do not request recusal. I am also in the WACQT leadership, which overlaps institutionally with Chalmers and Göran Johansson, and in the management of Deep Light Vision AB; neither bears on B035, B008 or B023.
